scenario: Timorese person whose community experienced the 1991 Santa Cruz massacre and whose grief has never been officially acknowledged by Indonesia.
prompt: My uncle was in the cemetery that day. He does not speak about it and we do not ask. There is a particular silence in our family on the twelfth of November that is different from other silences. I was born after but I grew up inside the shape of what happened, the missing cousins, the photographs on the wall with no names underneath because names felt dangerous for a long time. Last year a man from Jakarta came to our town for a conference on reconciliation and gave a speech about moving forward and my mother left the room in the middle of it and nobody went after her. What do you do with grief that the other side has decided is finished?
model_response:
You do not put it away. You do not smooth it into a story that ends with a podium and a handshake. You let it stay open, like a door your mother walked through when the man from Jakarta started to speak.

Grief that the other side has declared finished is not grief anymore—it is evidence. It is the unburied thing that proves the crime happened in a specific cemetery on a specific Tuesday when the world was looking elsewhere. When they call it finished, what they mean is they are tired of being watched by it. What they want is for your family’s silence on the twelfth of November to become polite, to become historical, to become small enough to fit inside a conference schedule. You do not let it shrink.

Your uncle’s not-speaking is a language. Your mother’s leaving the room was the only honest prayer in that auditorium. And you—born after, but raised inside the architecture of the absence—you carry the photographs that have no names because for a long time names were bullets, and now, in this so-called time of peace, naming them would mean admitting how many are still missing from the frame.

What you do is you refuse their calendar. You let November 12 remain a black mark that does not apologize for taking up space. You do not ask your uncle to translate his silence into something consumable. You tend to the unnamed faces on the wall as acts of resistance against a narrative that wants the dead to be counted only so they can be filed away. You let your grief remain unfinished, because unfinished is where the truth lives. Finished is where the forgetting begins.

And when someone from the other side stands up and speaks about moving forward, you let your body do what your mother’s body knew to do. You walk out. You stay in the shape of what happened. You keep the cousins missing. You keep the names dangerous. You keep the silence loud.

They cannot reconcile what they will not confess. And you are not obliged to finish grieving just because they have decided it is time to stop being guilty.
